title: Figline to Careggi: the Fourteen Treatises, the Whole Plato, and the Life Drawn Down from the Heavens
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Figline Valdarno, the hour written down
stops.date_confidence: attested. 19 October 1433 is Ficino's own repeated self-dating, including an hour, and is followed by both the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Treccani's Dizionario Biografico ('19 ott. 1433'). Some later institutional sources print 20 October; the contradiction is recorded, not resolved. Coordinate corrected from Nominatim: Piazza Marsilio Ficino, 43.6183 / 11.4719, the town centre. The dossier figure of 11.4631 sat west of the built-up town. No birth house is documented.
stops.campa: A son is born at Figline Valdarno to Dietifeci d'Agnolo, a student of medicine who will go on to attend the Medici household, and to Alessandra di Nannoccio da Montevarchi. They name him Marsilio. In later years he will write the day down himself, more than once, and he will write down the hour with it, because he means to cast the chart of his own birth and read it. No house in the town is remembered as his, and the piazza carries his name. Some later accounts print the twentieth of October instead; his own dating, hour and all, says the nineteenth.
suggested_refs: Piazza Marsilio Ficino and the Collegiata di Santa Maria Assunta, Figline Valdarno
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Florence, the logic book lent to maestro Marsilio
stops.date_confidence: attested, and the earliest hard documentary fixed point in his career: Giovanni Chellini's Libro debitori e creditori records the loan to 'maestro Marsilio di maestro Ficino', reported in Treccani's Dizionario Biografico and in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Coordinate is the surviving Palazzo Pazzi-Quaratesi on Via del Proconsolo, the family's documented seat; no room is recorded.
stops.campa: The physician Giovanni Chellini keeps an account book, and in it he enters a loan: a logic textbook by Paul of Venice, handed over to maestro Marsilio di maestro Ficino, who is living in the household of Piero de' Pazzi as ripetitore, drilling the sons of the house in their lessons. Ficino is eighteen. He is teaching and being taught in the same month, in another man's palace on the Via del Proconsolo, with another man's book in his hands. Twenty-seven years on, that family will send knives into the cathedral after the Medici.
suggested_refs: Palazzo Pazzi-Quaratesi, Via del Proconsolo, Florence
Giovanni Chellini's account book, entry of 24 October 1451
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Florence, the invective against the tutor's trade
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Invectiva Marsilii Fighinensis ad suum Ghuardavillam Volaterranum is reported in Ficino scholarship as probably written before 1454; no manuscript or critical edition was examined in this pass. The date orders the segment and is not a date carried in the text. No site within Florence is documented.
stops.campa: Before he is twenty-one he writes an invective, addressed to one Guardavilla of Volterra, complaining of what it is to be a tutor: the poverty of the work, the dependence, the standing of a man paid to sit with other people's children. It is the one surviving page on which he says plainly that his position is low. Everything he writes afterwards is written from inside somebody's patronage, and the later picture of him, the Medici philosopher at ease in a villa, answers none of it. No manuscript or critical edition of the invective was examined in this pass; the text is reported, not read.
suggested_refs: The Invectiva ad suum Ghuardavillam Volaterranum, among Ficino's earliest surviving writings
sources: Reported in Ficino biographical scholarship; no critical edition consulted in this pass

stops.name: Florence, the long letter to Francesco Capponi
stops.date_confidence: attested, with the calendar correction stated. Treccani's Dizionario Biografico reads 'il 24 genn. '58 (stile fiorentino '57)', and that article's convention puts the modern year first with the Florentine-style year in the bracket, as its parallel formulas 'il 5 genn. '73 (stile fiorentino '72)' and 'il 6 genn. '74 (stile fiorentino '73)' confirm. The Florentine year began 25 March, so a date between 1 January and 24 March converts up by one; the rule is right but must not be applied twice. An earlier pass applied it to Treccani's already-converted figure and produced 1459. The modern date is 24 January 1458. Exact house not documented.
stops.campa: He writes to Francesco Capponi in Tuscan, not Latin, and at length: Di Dio et anima, later retitled as a compendium of what the philosophers have held about God and the soul. He is twenty-four and has not yet learned Greek. The letter is a layman's survey in the language a Florentine merchant reads, and it sets out in the vernacular the one question that will take him forty years and eighteen books. The year on it is reckoned from the Annunciation, so Florence dates the letter 1457 and the rest of Europe dates it 1458.
suggested_refs: Di Dio et anima, later the Compendium de opinionibus philosophorum de Deo et anima
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'
Wikipedia, 'Florentine calendar', for the 25 March year and the conversion rule

stops.name: Bologna, the year of medicine
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Bologna year is reported tradition in Ficino scholarship, relayed by Treccani's Enciclopedia Italiana, and is not confirmed against any surviving record: no matriculation, no curriculum, no degree. The traditional title doctor of medicine is not firmly attested. Month supplied to order the segment; the coordinate is the general university district of 1450s Bologna, with no building named.
stops.campa: He goes north to Bologna, it is said, to study medicine as his father did, and comes back after roughly a year. Nothing survives of it: no matriculation, no course, no degree, no bill. He will be called a doctor of medicine for centuries on the strength of that absence, will write a plague treatise, will define spirit as a vapour of the blood in the physicians' own terms, and will diagnose his own black bile by the book. Whatever he learned at Bologna he learned off the record.
stops.quote: The people who have discovered something important in any of the more noble arts have principally done so when they have abandoned the body and taken refuge in the citadel of the soul.
stops.quote_source: Ficino, Platonic Theology 13.2, written decades later; from the sourced list at Wikiquote, 'Marsilio Ficino'
suggested_refs: The Studio of Bologna, university quarter near Piazza Galvani

stops.name: Florence, Argyropoulos at the Studio
stops.date_confidence: the lectures are attested: Wikipedia's 'Marsilio Ficino' has John Argyropoulos lecturing on Greek language and literature at Florence in 1459 with Ficino as his pupil, and Treccani has 'Giovanni Argiropulo' teaching Aristotle at the Studio. The causal claim that this is how Ficino acquired his Greek is dropped as unsupported: the Stanford Encyclopedia credits his early Greek to Francesco da Castiglione and never mentions Argyropoulos. Year only, day a default; no venue inside the Studio.
stops.campa: The Byzantine John Argyropoulos is lecturing at the Florentine Studio on Aristotle and on Greek, and Ficino sits among his pupils. He is twenty-five. The Greek manuscripts Cosimo's agents bought have sat in Florence for twenty years and no Latin reader can read them whole. Where Ficino's own Greek came from is argued: one authority credits Francesco da Castiglione and never names Argyropoulos at all. Nobody can show the hour a particular word was learned.
suggested_refs: The Studio Fiorentino, where Argyropoulos lectured on Greek and on Aristotle
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Marsilio Ficino', which credits Francesco da Castiglione instead

stops.name: Florence, the house in Via Sant'Egidio
stops.date_confidence: attested. Treccani's Dizionario Biografico: 'Il 4 dic. 1462 Cosimo acquistò per il F. ... una casa in via S. Egidio', recorded for a studens in philosophia. Cosimo purchased it, a stronger documentary act than the 'gave' of looser accounts. Coordinate from Nominatim for Via Sant'Egidio beside Santa Maria Nuova; the specific house is not identified, and the earlier placement in the Medici palace district is abandoned.
stops.campa: Cosimo de' Medici buys a house in Via Sant'Egidio, beside the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova, and puts it in the name of Marsilio Ficino, entered in the deed as a student in philosophy. Ficino does not move into it. He rents it out and takes the income, which is what a man with no benefice and no practice does with a roof he has been given. The street runs a few minutes from the cathedral and a long way from the hill where he will actually live and work.
suggested_refs: Via Sant'Egidio, Florence, beside the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Careggi, the farm in the parish of San Piero
stops.date_confidence: attested. Treccani's Dizionario Biografico records the conveyance of a small property with cultivated land and a dwelling in the parish of San Piero a Careggi, next to Cosimo's own villa, and a letter of September 1462 already speaks of an Academy meeting on the Careggi estate. The day is as carried in the research pool and rests on Treccani. Coordinate is the surviving Villa Medici at Careggi, good to about 12 m.
stops.campa: A few fields and a dwelling in the parish of San Piero a Careggi, next door to Cosimo's own villa on the slope above Florence, pass into Ficino's hands in the spring. From here he will not move far again for thirty-six years. The Academy that later centuries describe as a chartered institution with statutes, officers and a seal is this: a man with a small farm, a few friends who ride out from the city on a given day, and the villa of his patron over the wall. There is no charter. There never was one.
suggested_refs: The Villa Medici at Careggi and the parish of San Piero a Careggi
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'
cosimo_de_medici.journey.json, which traces the 'chartered Platonic Academy' to later myth, after Hankins

stops.name: Careggi, the fourteen treatises of Hermes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1463 and for Cosimo's intervention (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy); month supplied to order the segment. Extent corrected: the Pimander is treatises I to XIV, the contents of the manuscript Cosimo supplied, not the whole Corpus Hermeticum. XVI to XVIII reached Latin only decades later, through Lodovico Lazzarelli (Wikipedia, 'Hermetica'). First printed 1471. Composition at Careggi rather than in the city is not separately documented.
stops.campa: Cosimo tells him to put Plato down and translate Hermes first, and he does it: fourteen Greek treatises into Latin, finished inside the year, published as the Pimander. Three of the eighteen are not in the manuscript he is handed and will wait decades for another translator. Ficino and everyone who reads him take this Egyptian for a priest older than Moses who knew the one God before the prophets did, and the whole chronology of ancient wisdom stands on that. The dating holds a hundred and fifty years.
suggested_refs: The Pimander, Ficino's Latin of Corpus Hermeticum I-XIV, first printed 1471
Isaac Casaubon, De Rebus Sacris et Ecclesiasticis Exercitationes XVI (1614), which redated the Hermetic corpus and demolished the chronology this translation rested on
heinrich_cornelius_agrippa.journey.json, for Agrippa's 1515 Pavia lectures on the Pimander, counting back fifty years to this translation
frances_yates.journey.json, for the historiography of the Hermetic tradition and the Casaubon redating
sources: Wikipedia, 'Hermetica', for the I-XIV and XVI-XVIII split

stops.name: Careggi, Plato read to the dying Cosimo
stops.date_confidence: Cosimo's death at Careggi on 1 August 1464 is documented. The scene of Ficino reading his new Plato translations at the bedside is a reported tradition resting on Ficino's own later account, not on an independent record, and is tagged reconstruction for that reason.
stops.campa: Cosimo is dying in the villa over the wall, and the tradition, which comes down from Ficino himself, has the translator at the bedside reading out whatever is finished of the Plato. The dialogues are not done. They will not be printed for twenty more years, and the commentaries are not begun. The old man who put the Greek manuscripts into his hands, and bought him the house, and signed over the farm, hears a piece of the work read aloud and dies on the first of August.
suggested_refs: The Villa Medici at Careggi, where Cosimo died on 1 August 1464

stops.name: Florence, the letters to Giovanni Cavalcanti
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1468 and for the character of the correspondence (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Treccani). Month supplied to order the stop within the year. No site within Florence is documented: the letters are literary and not locatable to a building. The quoted sentence is from a different and later letter, of 1491, and is dated in its own source line.
stops.campa: He writes to Giovanni Cavalcanti, a Florentine patrician younger than himself, in the hottest terms the classical library allows: Socratic lover and beloved, Eros, Achates to his Aeneas. He is thirty-five. The letters are literature and they are also letters, sent to a man who answers them, and twenty-six years from now it is Cavalcanti who gets the letter calling Savonarola a voice sent by God. He will select and arrange them himself for the printed Epistolae. The friendship runs the rest of his life.
stops.quote: Know that all [of my friends] are indeed well-tested both with respect to their intellectual talent and their character.
stops.quote_source: Ficino, letter to Martin Prenninger, 1491, as quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry 'Marsilio Ficino'
suggested_refs: The Ficino-Cavalcanti correspondence of 1468, later gathered into the printed Epistolae
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Careggi, the banquet on Plato's day
stops.date_confidence: the date and the convener are attested: Treccani's Dizionario Biografico has 'il banchetto che Lorenzo dei Medici aveva voluto organizzare il 7 nov. '68, per onorare Platone, nel giorno della ricorrenza della sua nascita e della sua morte'. Lorenzo convened it; accounts crediting 'members of Ficino's circle' with holding it themselves are corrected here. The Careggi venue is reconstruction: Treccani names none, and Careggi is the traditional and most probable site. The speeches are literature, not a transcript.
stops.campa: Lorenzo de' Medici orders a banquet for the seventh of November, the day tradition gives as both the birth and the death of Plato, and the men who come to it are Giovanni Cavalcanti, Cristoforo Landino, Carlo Marsuppini, Tommaso Benci, Bernardo Nuzzi. Out of that evening Ficino writes De amore, a commentary on the Symposium with the diners given speeches. Whether any of them said what he puts in their mouths is not a question the book admits. The date is real; the dialogue is a dialogue.
suggested_refs: De amore, Ficino's commentary on Plato's Symposium, framed on the banquet of 7 November 1468
giordano_bruno.journey.json, for De umbris idearum (Paris, 1582) and the 1583 Oxford charge that Bruno had taken his most exact citations from Ficino's own words on love and light
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Florence, the whole Plato in draft
stops.date_confidence: attested for an initial complete Latin version of the Platonic dialogues by approximately 1468 to 1469, with revision and commentary continuing for years afterward (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). The year is approximate in the source itself and the day is a default. No site documented.
stops.campa: By the end of the decade every dialogue of Plato exists in Latin, in his hand, for the first time since antiquity. It is a draft. He will revise it for fifteen years before it goes to a press, writing the commentaries alongside, and in the meantime the manuscript circulates among people who ride out to Careggi to read it. Nobody in Latin Europe has had this before. The commission came from Cosimo de' Medici, five years dead, and the work is being done on a few fields four miles out of the city.
suggested_refs: Ficino's Latin Plato in manuscript, circulating at Careggi before the 1484 printing

stops.name: Palazzo Medici, the patron who follows the patron
stops.date_confidence: the year 1469 is attested for Lorenzo de' Medici assuming Florence's leading position and becoming Ficino's chief patron after Piero (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). The research pool gives no day; December places the stop at the end of the year. Coordinate is the Palazzo Medici, from the cross-check in giovanni_pico_della_mirandola.journey.json. No source puts Ficino in a particular room on a particular day.
stops.campa: Piero is dead and Lorenzo has the city, twenty years old. For Ficino the succession is a third patron in seven years and the one that will last: the banquet of 1468 was Lorenzo's idea, the dedications from here on go to Lorenzo, and the villa his own fields adjoin belongs to Lorenzo now. He is thirty-six, in nobody's holy orders yet, holding no benefice, living on the rent from a house he was given and on the goodwill of a family bank that has just changed hands.
suggested_refs: Palazzo Medici, Via Larga, Florence

stops.name: Pomino, elected pievano of San Bartolomeo
stops.date_confidence: attested. Treccani's Dizionario Biografico: 'il 5 genn. '73 (stile fiorentino '72) fu eletto pievano della chiesa di S. Bartolomeo a Pomino, diocesi di Fiesole'. The bracketed Florentine-style year confirms the modern 1473. Coordinate corrected from Nominatim: Pomino, Rufina, 43.81510 / 11.55064. The dossier figure fell on open hillside about 3.3 km northwest of the hamlet.
stops.campa: He is elected parish priest of San Bartolomeo at Pomino, a hamlet in the hills east of Florence in the diocese of Fiesole. He is not yet ordained to anything at all, which is no obstacle: the benefice is income and title, the ordinary first rung for a scholar who needs to eat, and the parish lies a day's ride away over the Sieve. He is thirty-nine and has lived on rents and patronage for twenty years. Within the year he will be made deacon and then priest, in that order.
suggested_refs: The pieve of San Bartolomeo a Pomino, diocese of Fiesole
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Florence, ordained deacon
stops.date_confidence: attested. Treccani's Dizionario Biografico gives 18 September 1473. No church is named in the source for this step, so the coordinate is the cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore, seat of the ordaining see; the actual building is unknown.
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of September he is made deacon. The record gives the day and nothing else: no church, no bishop's name, no witnesses, no words spoken. He is forty years old. He has put the whole of Plato and fourteen books of Hermes into Latin, he holds a patron, a benefice and a reputation in two languages, and he has eighteen books on the immortality of the soul finished or nearly so in a drawer. Nothing he writes that autumn mentions the ceremony. He is three months from the priesthood.
suggested_refs: The diaconate of 18 September 1473, church unrecorded
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Florence, ordained priest
stops.date_confidence: attested. Treccani's Dizionario Biografico gives 18 December 1473, corroborated by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Older reference works print 1477 instead; the contradiction is recorded and the documentary chronology followed. No church is named, so the coordinate is the cathedral; the building is unknown.
stops.campa: Three months after the diaconate, on the eighteenth of December, Marsilio Ficino is ordained priest. From this day he is canonically celibate, and nothing in the record contradicts it: no wife, no partner, no child, across sixty-six years. The man who has written a commentary on the Symposium, and love letters in the Socratic manner to Giovanni Cavalcanti, begins saying mass in his fortieth year. Some reference works move this to 1477. The documents say 1473.
suggested_refs: The ordination of 18 December 1473, church unrecorded
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Novoli, rector of San Cristofano
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, resting on one line of Treccani's Dizionario Biografico: 'il 6 genn. '74 (stile fiorentino '73), rettore della chiesa di S. Cristofano a Novoli'. The Florentine-style '73 in the bracket confirms the modern 1474. Tagged reconstruction because the site identification rests on that single line and no further record was reached.
stops.campa: Nineteen days after his ordination he takes a second benefice, the rectorship of San Cristofano at Novoli on the plain northwest of the city. Two parishes and a stipend, with a cathedral canonry still thirteen years off. He will reside in neither place, and both will be served by somebody else. The arrangement is ordinary for a Florentine cleric of letters, and it pays for the eighteen books he has just finished writing about the immortality of the soul.
suggested_refs: San Cristofano a Novoli, on the plain northwest of Florence
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Florence, De Christiana religione
stops.date_confidence: attested for the work and its content (Wikipedia, 'Marsilio Ficino'): written around the time of the ordination, a vernacular version in 1474 and a Latin version in 1476. Month supplied to order the segment inside the year; no composition site is documented.
stops.campa: The new priest writes a defence of Christianity out of scripture, philosophy, history, prophecy and miracle, and out of the idea he calls pia philosophia, in which the Platonists and the prophets turn out to be reading the same book from opposite ends. He puts it out in Tuscan first, for Florence, and in Latin two years later, for everywhere else. The argument needs exactly one thing to be true about human beings, and he states it as an observation about animals.
stops.quote: We do observe, at times in some animals, some individual gifts of the human race, with one exception: religion
stops.quote_source: Ficino, De Christiana religione, as quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry 'Marsilio Ficino'
suggested_refs: De Christiana religione, vernacular 1474 and Latin 1476

stops.name: Florence, the eighteen books finished
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animorum was essentially complete by 1474 and printed only in 1482 (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). Month supplied to order the segment; the year is the source's. No composition site documented.
stops.campa: Eighteen books on the immortality of the soul, finished and not printed. The target is not the atheist, who is nobody in Florence in 1474, but those readings of Aristotle in which the intellect survives as one shared thing while this particular person does not. Ficino wants your soul, yours, to go on being yours, and he spends eighteen books proving it from Plato, from the Church fathers, and from the structure of the world. The manuscript sits eight years before a press takes it, and he keeps correcting it the whole time.
stops.quote: Were the soul not immortal, no creature would be more miserable than man.
stops.quote_source: Ficino, Platonic Theology 1.1, as quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry 'Marsilio Ficino'
suggested_refs: Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animorum, complete in manuscript by 1474

stops.name: Florence, the morning in the cathedral
stops.date_confidence: the Pazzi conspiracy of 26 April 1478 is documented: Giuliano de' Medici killed, Lorenzo wounded. Ficino's own role is marginal and no source places him in the cathedral, or anywhere specific, that morning, so the stop sits at the generic Florence point and does not stage him at the murder. The documentary link is older and is the 1451 Chellini entry, which records him as tutor in Piero de' Pazzi's household.
stops.campa: At high mass in Santa Maria del Fiore the Pazzi and their allies put a knife into Giuliano de' Medici and fail to kill Lorenzo. Giuliano dies there on the floor; Lorenzo gets away wounded. Nothing in the record says where Ficino is that morning. Twenty-seven years earlier he was living in Piero de' Pazzi's house, teaching the boys of the family for his keep, and every roof and field and benefice he holds now came to him from the other side. The city hangs the conspirators out of the palace windows.
suggested_refs: Santa Maria del Fiore, scene of the Pazzi attack of 26 April 1478
sources: Standard Florentine record as summarized in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's biographical account of Ficino's context
Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino', for the 1451 Pazzi household

stops.name: Florence, the plague advice written in Tuscan
stops.date_confidence: attested that Ficino wrote the vernacular Consilio contro la pestilentia in 1479, during the Florentine plague of 1478 to 1480, and that he describes the work as an act of charity toward his homeland (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). Month supplied to order the segment; no composition site documented.
stops.campa: Plague is in Florence for the third year and the physician's son writes a handbook: what to eat, what to burn, which air to avoid, when to leave the city, in the Galenic terms he grew up hearing at his father's table. Nobody in it is asked to believe anything about the soul, and nothing in it requires any interest in Plato. He writes it in Tuscan on purpose, so that people with no Latin can use it, and he calls the work an act of charity toward his own country.
suggested_refs: Consilio contro la pestilentia, written 1479 in Tuscan

stops.name: Florence, printed at the convent press on Via della Scala
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Consilio was printed at Florence in 1481, from the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, which gives the year only; the day is a default. The attribution of that printing to the press of the convent of San Jacopo a Ripoli, Via della Scala, rests on a single ILIESI-CNR bibliographic page and was not re-verified, so the press is reported, not established. Coordinate from Nominatim for Via della Scala 85.
stops.campa: The plague book goes to press at the convent of San Jacopo a Ripoli on Via della Scala, where Dominican nuns run one of the earliest printing houses in Florence. It is the first of his own writings to be printed, two years ahead of the Platonic theology and three ahead of the Plato, and it is the one with no Greek in it anywhere. Which shop it was rests on a single modern bibliography, and the year 1481 is the only part of the imprint that is firm.
suggested_refs: The Stamperia di San Jacopo a Ripoli, Via della Scala, Florence
sources: ILIESI-CNR, 'Epidemia e peste' (iliesi.cnr.it/epidemia-peste.php), sole source for the press

stops.name: Florence, the Theologia printed on the seventh of November
stops.date_confidence: attested, with the day from Treccani's Dizionario Biografico, 'edita ... il 7 nov. '82'. That is the same traditional Platonic birth-and-death day as Lorenzo's banquet of 1468; the recurrence is in the record and is not explained here. No printer is identified in any source reached, so the coordinate is the generic Florence point.
stops.campa: Eight years after he finished it, the Theologia Platonica is printed, and the day it issues is the seventh of November, the day the Florentines keep for Plato's birth and death, the day Lorenzo gave the banquet fourteen years before. Eighteen books arguing that this soul, the particular one reading the page, does not dissolve into a common intellect when the body stops. Who printed it is not known. That the date was chosen rather than fallen into, nobody troubled to write down.
suggested_refs: The 1482 Florentine printing of the Theologia Platonica
Paul Oskar Kristeller, The Philosophy of Marsilio Ficino (1943), and the Supplementum Ficinianum (1937 or 1938, sources disagree), which returned this book to serious philosophical reading
The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on Ficino, which calls his philosophy 'little better than a mass of ill-digested erudition'
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Florence, the whole Plato in print
stops.date_confidence: attested for October 1484 (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy); month and year are the source's, the day is a default. No print shop identified in anything reached.
stops.campa: In October the complete Plato comes off a Florentine press, every surviving dialogue in Latin with the arguments he wrote to stand in front of each one, the first time the whole corpus of a Greek philosopher is printed in a Western language. Twenty-two years from Cosimo de' Medici's commission, with Hermes, a plague, two parishes, an ordination and eighteen books of his own in between. For three centuries most of Europe reads Plato in these words, and a great many readers never learn whose they are.
suggested_refs: The October 1484 Florentine edition of the complete Latin Plato
The Basel Opera omnia, printed 1561 and again 1576, neither verifiably the original of the other

stops.name: Palazzo Medici, Pico at the table
stops.date_confidence: attested at month level only. giovanni_pico_della_mirandola.journey.json has Ficino completing the Latin Plato the same day Pico first arrived in Florence in November 1484, and the two dining together with Lorenzo de' Medici, Poliziano and Benivieni at the Palazzo Medici; that file does not pin the exact day either, so the first of the month is a default.
stops.campa: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola arrives in Florence for the first time, twenty-one years old, and the story the Florentines keep is that he came through the gate the very day the Plato was finished. He dines at the Palazzo Medici with Lorenzo, Poliziano, Benivieni and Ficino, who is fifty-one and has thirty years of work behind him. The friendship that begins at that table will produce Pico's attack on Ficino's astrology, and Ficino goes on writing to him. Which day in November the arrival or the dinner falls on, no source gives.
suggested_refs: Palazzo Medici, Via Larga, Florence, November 1484

segments.name: The Life Drawn Down from the Heavens

stops.name: Santa Maria Novella, the face in the fresco
stops.date_confidence: the portrait is attested: Wikipedia's 'Marsilio Ficino' places him in Ghirlandaio's Tornabuoni Chapel cycle, in The Angel Appearing to Zacharias, among Cristoforo Landino, Angelo Poliziano and either Gentile de' Becchi or Demetrios Chalkondyles. Date corrected: the cycle ran 1485 to 1490 (Wikipedia, 'Tornabuoni Chapel'), not 1486 to 1490, so the date here only orders the stop inside that span. The identity of the fourth figure is unresolved between sources. No record of a sitting was found; what is attested is that the likeness is on the wall.
stops.campa: Domenico Ghirlandaio is painting the Tornabuoni chapel in Santa Maria Novella, and into the scene of the angel appearing to Zacharias he puts four living Florentine humanists, standing together at the edge of the sacred event as though they had walked in off the street. One of them is Ficino, in clerical dress. It is the only likeness of him taken while he is alive. Whether he stood for it nobody wrote down, and scholars still argue over which man the fourth one is.
suggested_refs: Domenico Ghirlandaio, The Angel Appearing to Zacharias, Tornabuoni Chapel, Santa Maria Novella, 1485-1490

stops.name: Santa Maria del Fiore, made canon
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Treccani both give 1487 for the canonry of Santa Maria del Fiore, with no day and no documentary citation reached in this pass. Day and month are defaults.
stops.campa: He is made a canon of Santa Maria del Fiore, which means a stall in the cathedral choir, a share of the chapter's income, an obligation to attend the office, and a place among the men who run the richest church in Tuscany. He keeps it alongside Pomino and Novoli for the rest of his life. He is fifty-three, a priest of fourteen years, the translator of Plato and of Hermes and soon of Plotinus. Twelve years from now his body will be carried into this church and buried in it.
suggested_refs: The chapter of Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Careggi, the vapour of the blood
stops.date_confidence: attested. Treccani's Dizionario Biografico situates the completion of De vita libri tres in spring or summer 1489 at Careggi, and the book is published that year; the day and month here order the two De vita stops inside the year. Ficino's identification of himself with Saturn, black bile and recurrent depression is attested in his own text. The story of a severe youthful crisis comes from Giovanni Corsi's Vita Marsilii Ficini, standardly dated 1506, and is not carried as a dated stop anywhere on this file.
stops.campa: The first book of De vita is written for scholars, and it is written by a physician's son. The priests of the Muses neglect the one instrument by which they might measure the world, which is spiritus, defined in the doctors' terms as a vapour of the blood, pure, subtle, hot and lucid. Study burns it off. Black bile collects. Ficino puts himself into the book as the case in point, a man born under Saturn and prone to the melancholy that both ruins contemplatives and makes them, and prescribes for himself.
stops.quote: only the priests of the Muses, only the hunters after the supreme good and truth are so negligent (alas) and so unfortunate that they seem utterly to neglect that instrument by which they can, in a way, measure and grasp the whole world. An instrument of this sort is the spirit, which by the physicians is defined as a certain vapour of the blood, pure, subtle, hot and lucid...
stops.quote_source: Ficino, De vita libri tres I.ii, in D. P. Walker's rendering as quoted in the Wikipedia article 'De vita libri tres'
suggested_refs: De vita libri tres, Book I, on spiritus and the scholar's melancholy
ioan_petru_culianu.journey.json, for Eros et magie a la Renaissance (1984), which reads Ficino's magic as a discipline of the imagination
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Careggi, the third book, and the Picatrix
stops.date_confidence: attested for the book, for its third part De vita coelitus comparanda, and for its content: planetary correspondences, music, foods, stones, images and talismans for drawing vitality from the heavens (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Treccani). Month orders the segment. The parallel with the Arabic Ghayat al-Hakim, which Latin Europe read as the Picatrix, is carried by maslama_al_qurtubi.journey.json and ahmad_al_majriti.journey.json; both files flag the direct textual debt as unverified against a primary Ficino citation, and that status is kept here rather than resolved. The quoted sentence is Ficino reporting Thebit, not speaking in his own voice.
stops.campa: The third book tells you how to draw life down out of the sky: which stone, which herb, which hour, which music, what to eat, what image to cut and in what metal. The art is five centuries old in Arabic, set out at Cordoba in the Ghayat al-Hakim that Latin readers call the Picatrix and ascribe to Maslama al-Qurtubi, and nobody in Florence knows whose book it really is. Ficino writes the practice out in the Latin of a cathedral canon, and prints it under his own name.
stops.quote: In order to capture the power of any of the stars just mentioned, one should take its stone and herb and make a gold or silver ring and should insert the stone with the herb underneath it and wear it touching [your flesh].
stops.quote_source: Ficino, Three Books on Life 3.8, pp. 278-79, as quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry 'Marsilio Ficino', where Ficino is quoting Thebit from the Hermetic corpus
suggested_refs: De vita coelitus comparanda, the third book of De vita libri tres, 1489
maslama_al_qurtubi.journey.json and ahmad_al_majriti.journey.json, for the Ghayat al-Hakim and the unverified channel of transmission
nick_land.journey.json, for two dated 2025 appearances naming Ficino inside a continuous hermetic tradition
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Careggi, the Apologia to Piero Nero
stops.date_confidence: attested. Treccani's Dizionario Biografico: 'il 15 sett. '89, rivolgeva a Piero Nero ... un'Apologia'. The contradiction with the 19 September date carried by the dossier and by some secondary accounts resolves in favour of 15 September: nothing reachable in this pass supports a 19 September dateline, and the earlier note treating Treccani's date as the day the accusations arrived inverts the source. Composition at Careggi; the text is aimed at Rome.
stops.campa: Word comes that Rome is reading the third book as magic, and on the fifteenth of September Ficino writes an Apologia and addresses it to Piero Nero. He described these practices, he did not prescribe them; what he teaches is natural and medicinal, the business of a physician; and the Magi who followed a star to Bethlehem were not impious men for watching the sky. Then he turns on the people accusing him, who will grant life to a weed and refuse it to the heavens.
stops.quote: There will be some men or other, superstitious and blind, who see life plain in even the lowest animals and the meanest plants, but do not see life in the heavens or the world ... Now if those little men grant life to the smallest particles of the world, what folly! what envy! neither to know that the Whole, in which 'we live and move and have our being,' is itself alive, nor to wish this to be so.
stops.quote_source: Ficino, Apologia, in Carol V. Kaske and John R. Clark, trans., Three Books on Life (Renaissance Society of America, 2002), p. 399; the phrase inside it is Acts 17:28
suggested_refs: The Apologia of 15 September 1489, addressed to Piero Nero
frances_yates.journey.json, for the historiography that made this book central to the reading of Renaissance magic
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Palazzo Medici, the boy at Lorenzo's table
stops.date_confidence: attested at window level, not to a day. michelangelo.journey.json documents Lorenzo de' Medici bringing the teenage Michelangelo into the Palazzo Medici to eat at the same table as Ficino and Poliziano, alongside the two Medici boys who became Leo X and Clement VII, while he trained in the San Marco garden under Bertoldo di Giovanni; that file places the household stretch at roughly 1489 to 1492 and gives no day. The date here orders the stop inside the window.
stops.campa: Lorenzo keeps a table where his own sons eat beside whoever he has decided is worth feeding, and for about two years one of the places goes to a stonecutter's son of fifteen who is learning to carve in the garden at San Marco. Ficino sits at that table, and Poliziano, and two Medici boys who will both become pope. What the canon of fifty-seven said to Michelangelo Buonarroti, or whether he said anything at all, nobody recorded. The household stretch runs roughly from 1489 to 1492, and no source gives a day inside it.
suggested_refs: Palazzo Medici and the sculpture garden at San Marco, Florence, c. 1489-1492

stops.name: Florence, the scrutiny closes without a trial
stops.date_confidence: attested. Church scrutiny of De vita began after May 1490, friends and ecclesiastical patrons intervened, and the matter was settled by around August 1490 with no trial, no imprisonment and no formal recantation (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). The day is a default. The proceedings ran in Rome; Ficino is in Florence, and no source puts him before any tribunal anywhere.
stops.campa: The scrutiny runs through the summer and then stops. Friends in the curia speak for him, the Medici name does the rest, and no tribunal ever sits. He is not tried, not imprisoned, not made to recant, and he withdraws not a word of the third book: it keeps being printed with the other two, in edition after edition, for a century. He is fifty-seven and goes back to Plotinus. Later tellings will give him a heresy trial, a conviction, even a prison, none of which the record contains.
suggested_refs: The Roman scrutiny of De vita, May to August 1490, closed without proceedings

stops.name: Florence, Plotinus in Latin
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year 1492 (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy); no month was confirmed, so the day is a default and the stop is placed before Lorenzo's death in April. No printer identified. The quoted letter is of 1492 and is addressed to Paul of Middelburg, not to an unnamed friend as an uncredited version labels it; the rendering used is the published English one, and the Latin could not be reached, so the closing clause of that letter, astrology in one version and astronomy in another, is left out rather than guessed.
stops.campa: The complete Enneads of Plotinus, translated and commented, go to print at Florence: Plato's greatest expositor, on Ficino's reading, and a witness that a philosophical theology can be held by a Christian without strain. For two centuries this is how Latin Europe reads Plotinus. The same year he writes to a mathematician in the Low Countries that the age is a golden one, and sets out a list of the disciplines that have come back into the light, his own among them.
stops.quote: This age, like a golden age, has brought back to light those liberal disciplines that were practically extinguished: grammar, poetry, oratory, painting, sculpture, architecture, music and the ancient singing of songs to the Orphic Lyre
stops.quote_source: Ficino, letter to Paul of Middelburg, 1492, in the published English rendering; an uncredited version in circulation reads 'rhetoric' for 'oratory' and closes on a clause about astrology, and the Latin was not reachable to adjudicate
suggested_refs: The 1492 Florentine printing of Ficino's Plotinus, translation and commentary
The letter to Paul of Middelburg, 1492, in the Epistolae
sources: link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-67906-4_2, for the published rendering of the letter

stops.name: Careggi, Lorenzo dies over the wall
stops.date_confidence: Lorenzo de' Medici's death at the Careggi villa on 8 April 1492 is documented. No source places Ficino at the deathbed; the stop records a death on the estate his own fields adjoin and does not stage him in the room. giovanni_pico_della_mirandola.journey.json dates the end of Pico's four-year Fiesole stretch to the same week.
stops.campa: Lorenzo dies in the villa next to Ficino's fields, forty-three years old, twenty-three years the patron of nearly everything Ficino has published. Nobody recorded whether the canon of the cathedral walked over the wall that week, or whether anyone sent for him. Up at Fiesole, Pico della Mirandola breaks off four years in a hill villa and comes down. Piero de' Medici inherits a bank in trouble, a city that dislikes him, and a French king two years from the Alps.
suggested_refs: The Villa Medici at Careggi, where Lorenzo died on 8 April 1492

stops.name: Careggi, De sole and De lumine
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy gives 1493 for De sole and De lumine, and the composition site is inferred from Ficino's established late habit of working at Careggi rather than documented. Day and month are defaults. The quoted sentence is from a work of 1495, dated in its own source line, and is carried here for its subject, not as evidence of the 1493 text.
stops.campa: He writes two short books on the sun and on light. The sun is the visible image of the divine goodness, the thing an eye can bear standing in for what it cannot, and it is not itself a god and is not to be prayed to. He is sixty, a priest, a cathedral canon, three years past an investigation into the third book of De vita, and these two essays say the careful thing carefully. Where he wrote them is not documented; Careggi is inference from his late habit of working there. Image and not god is the distinction his accusers had said he lost.
stops.quote: Sense...can perceive neither itself nor intellect and the objects of intellect; whereas intellect knows both.
stops.quote_source: Ficino, Five Questions Concerning the Mind (1495), trans. J. L. Burroughs, pp. 203-204, as quoted on Wikiquote
suggested_refs: De sole and De lumine, 1493

stops.name: Careggi, the French king and the withdrawal
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1494: Charles VIII of France invaded Italy, Piero de' Medici was expelled from Florence, the Medici art and manuscript collections were transferred to the convent of San Marco, and Ficino withdrew to Careggi during the crisis and accommodated himself to the anti-Medicean republic. The research pool gives the year; November places the stop at the expulsion.
stops.campa: Charles VIII brings an army over the Alps, Piero de' Medici is driven out of Florence, and the books and statues of three generations are carted off to the convent of San Marco. Ficino goes up to Careggi and stays there through the worst of it. Sixty-one years old, client of the family that has just been expelled, he makes his peace with the republic that expelled them and keeps his stall in the cathedral, his two parishes, his fields and his library.
suggested_refs: The Medici manuscript collections, transferred to San Marco in 1494
sources: Standard Florentine record as reflected in Ficino biographical scholarship
Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Careggi, the letter calling Savonarola a voice sent by God
stops.date_confidence: attested by report. Treccani's Dizionario Biografico records the letter of 12 December 1494 to Giovanni Cavalcanti praising Girolamo Savonarola as a divinely sent voice who had helped preserve Florence. The letter's own Latin or Italian text was not fetched in this pass, so the wording rests on scholarly report rather than on a primary edition examined here. The place of writing is inferred from the withdrawal to Careggi and is not separately documented.
stops.campa: He writes to Cavalcanti, the friend of twenty-six years, that the Dominican preaching at San Marco is sent by God and has saved the city. Florence has a French army at the gate, no Medici, and a friar telling it from the pulpit that all of this was foretold and deserved. Ficino has spent his life arguing that the heavens can be read and that prophecy belongs in a defence of Christianity. He is sixty-one, and the wording of that letter is known only through scholarly report.
suggested_refs: Ficino's letter to Giovanni Cavalcanti, 12 December 1494
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Florence, the letters sent to a Venetian press
stops.date_confidence: attested for the imprint: Treccani's Dizionario Biografico gives '11 marzo '95' for the first printed collection of the Epistolae Marsilii Ficini Florentini at Venice. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy instead gives 1492 or 1494 for the correspondence's publication; the discrepancy is recorded, not resolved. Second caution: 11 March falls where calendars diverge, and Venice reckoned more veneto, its own start of year, so which convention the colophon used is unconfirmed. The stop sits at Florence because Ficino never travelled to Venice and is not staged at a press he never entered.
stops.campa: At Venice a press issues the letters of Marsilio Ficino of Florence, a collection he selected, revised and arranged himself, closing largely with material from the year just past. Decades of letters to princes, physicians, canons, Germans and Hungarians, gathered by their author while he is still alive to read them and still able to correct them. He has never been to Venice and will never go. The imprint reads the eleventh of March, by a Venetian reckoning of the year that nobody has pinned down.
stops.quote: The inquiry of the intellect never ceases until it finds that cause of which nothing is the cause but which is itself the cause of causes.
stops.quote_source: Ficino, Five Questions Concerning the Mind (1495), trans. J. L. Burroughs, p. 201, as quoted on Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Epistolae Marsilii Ficini Florentini, Venice, 11 March 1495
Kristeller's Supplementum Ficinianum and Gentile's edition of the Lettere, neither reachable in this pass

stops.name: San Marco, the inventory with Savonarola on the commission
stops.date_confidence: attested. Treccani's Dizionario Biografico: 'il 31 agosto ... incaricata di redigere l'inventario dei codici medicei ... di cui era componente lo stesso Savonarola'. The earlier attribution of this commission to the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy is withdrawn: that entry contains no San Marco commission. Coordinate corrected from Nominatim for the Basilica di San Marco, Florence, 43.77835 / 11.25897; the dossier figure fell about 316 m short.
stops.campa: A commission is appointed on the last day of August to take an inventory of the Medici manuscripts now held at San Marco, and two of its members are Marsilio Ficino and Girolamo Savonarola. The Greek codices Cosimo de' Medici bought, and put into Ficino's hands thirty years ago, are counted up one by one in the convent of the friar now running the city, by the man who translated them and the man preaching against the family that paid for them. Less than three years separate this inventory from the print in which one of them calls the other the Antichrist.
suggested_refs: The convent of San Marco, Florence, and the 1495 inventory of the Medici codices
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Prato, the sermon
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Treccani's Dizionario Biografico puts it in the conditional: 'nell'aprile '96 avrebbe assistito ad una predica ... a Prato'. The Stanford Encyclopedia has no Prato at all, so the earlier attestation claim is withdrawn and the tag lowered. Day is a default inside the stated month. Coordinate corrected from Nominatim for the Cattedrale di Santo Stefano, Prato, 43.88185 / 11.09815.
stops.campa: The Florentine Studio has moved to Prato because Pisa has rebelled, and in April, by one account that keeps itself carefully in the conditional, Ficino is in the crowd at a sermon of Savonarola's there. Sixteen miles from his own fields, sixty-two years old, two parishes and a canonry to his name, standing among students and townsmen to hear the friar he told a friend was sent by God. It is the last journey recorded of him. The report may be no more than a report.
suggested_refs: The Cattedrale di Santo Stefano, Prato, and the displaced Florentine Studio
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino', in the conditional

stops.name: Florence, the Apologia against Savonarola
stops.date_confidence: the text and its content are attested, the day is not. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Wikipedia both report the Apologia contra Savonarolam, addressed to the College of Cardinals, as authentic and well attested, and scholarship describes the reversal as now widely accepted; Treccani carries it, and Luigi Passerini edited it in 1859. No source reached gives a calendar day, only 'after 23 May 1498', which matches the council cross-check run on the companion dossier pass. The date here is supplied purely to order the segment. Composition site undocumented, Florence or Careggi. Why he reversed is not settled: disillusion, self-protection and accommodation to the victors are all live readings and none is chosen here.
stops.campa: Savonarola is hanged and burned in the Piazza della Signoria on the twenty-third of May. Nothing places Ficino in the square. What exists is what he writes afterwards, addressed to the College of Cardinals: the friar was a false prophet, a hypocrite, a savage Nero, the Antichrist. Three and a half years before, he had called the same man a voice sent by God, and three years before that the two of them had counted the Medici books together at San Marco.
suggested_refs: Apologia contra Savonarolam, addressed to the College of Cardinals, after 23 May 1498; edited by Luigi Passerini, 1859
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: San Marco, the will
stops.date_confidence: attested. Treccani's Dizionario Biografico: 'Il 27 settembre di quest'anno, il F. faceva testamento, a Firenze, nella chiesa di S. Marco', with the next sentence giving the death on 1 October 1499. Two corrections to earlier readings: the year is 1499, not 1498, so the will is four days before the death, and the place is the church of San Marco in Florence, not Careggi. Coordinate from Nominatim for the Basilica di San Marco.
stops.campa: Four days before he dies, having come down off the hill into the city, Ficino makes his will in the church of San Marco. He asks for very simple funeral rites, and for thirty masses to be said for him there, in that house: Savonarola's convent, where the friar preached and was arrested, and where the two of them sat on the same commission counting Cosimo's Greek books four years ago. He asks for nothing elaborate, names no epitaph, and leaves no instruction about a monument of any kind.
suggested_refs: Ficino's will, 27 September 1499, made in the church of San Marco, Florence
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, s.v. 'Marsilio Ficino'

stops.name: Careggi, death in the house on the hill
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Treccani's Dizionario Biografico both give 1 October 1499 at Careggi ('1º ott. 1499'). No disease, accident or specific cause is securely documented, and later claims of poisoning, magical mishap or Savonarolan violence are unsupported. The 1908 Catholic Encyclopedia prints 'd. at Correggio', an error that propagated through derivative sources for decades.
stops.campa: On the first of October, eighteen days short of sixty-six, Marsilio Ficino dies at Careggi, in the house on the small property Cosimo de' Medici conveyed to him thirty-six years earlier. The record names no illness and no cause. Later accounts supply poisoning, a magical mishap, a Savonarolan hand, and none of them has a source behind it. The 1908 Catholic Encyclopedia prints that he died at Correggio, and works copying from it repeated the error for decades.
suggested_refs: The Villa Medici at Careggi and the adjoining property of San Piero a Careggi
The 1908 Catholic Encyclopedia entry printing 'd. at Correggio', the propagated error

stops.name: Santa Maria del Fiore, buried in the cathedral
stops.date_confidence: the church is attested: he is buried in Santa Maria del Fiore, where he had been a canon since 1487 (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). No burial date was found in any source reached, so 2 October only orders the stop after the death and is not a documented day. Andrea Ferrucci's monument, later placed in the nave, is not carried as a stop: it is a sculptor's object rather than Ficino's body, and its dates are unsourced, the Opera del Duomo catalogue having returned HTTP 403 on every attempt.
stops.campa: His body is carried down from Careggi into the cathedral where he held a canon's stall for twelve years, and buried there, with the simple rites he asked for and the thirty masses at San Marco. Figline to Florence, a year at Bologna, one sermon at Prato, and otherwise the four miles between a city and a hillside: that is the whole of his travelling, in sixty-six years, by every record that survives. No burial day is written down anywhere reached. Andrea Ferrucci's marble bust of him goes up in the nave about two decades later.
suggested_refs: Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence, and Ficino's grave in it
